posts.raw_content:
Most Americans still have no idea what artificial intelligence can actually do.

Their experience with AI largely begins and ends with the viral frenzy of 2022 when they opened ChatGPT asked it to write a poem or make a joke, played around with image generators, and then moved on with their lives. That version of AI is already ancient history. The technology has advanced at an extraordinary pace and today these systems can research, write, analyze documents, control and do anything on your computer, generate software, automate workflows, create media, and increasingly operate as agents capable of completing complicated tasks with limited supervision. The gap between what AI can actually do and what the average American thinks it can do has become enormous.

At the same time public hostility toward the infrastructure powering this technology is growing rapidly. Across the country communities are organizing against massive data center projects, raising concerns about electricity prices, water consumption, noise, land use, and the strain these facilities can place on local infrastructure. The technology industry tends to dismiss these people as those who do not understand progress, but I think that completely misses the point. Americans are not necessarily rejecting technology. They are rejecting a technology industry they no longer trust, and in many cases that industry has done very little to earn their trust. The problem is Silicon Valley itself, not even necessarily the data centers.

The fundamental problem is that Silicon Valley often views communities through the lens of efficiency rather than human flourishing. A technology executive looks at a rural county and see cheap land, available megawatts, transmission capacity, tax incentives, and water access. The people who live there see their home. If a corporation arrives, drops a massive industrial complex into a community, consumes enormous amounts of power and water, changes the landscape, and potentially raises costs while offering residents little obvious benefit, it should not be surprising when people push back.

You cannot continually ask ordinary Americans to absorb the downside of technological development while the upside flows primarily to enormous corporations hundreds or thousands of miles away. You need to tell them what is actually in it for them. What are the tangible benefits? Will their towns be generating massive amounts of tax revenue? Will they get a dividend on profits from that data center so they can better provide for their families? Will the company running the data center pledge millions of dollars towards improving the local community and building new schools, parks, etc?

This is why I believe the debate over data centers is ultimately a debate about purpose. Technology should serve people, families, communities, and the nation. It should help a father provide for his family, help a small business compete with a larger corporation, help a builder work more efficiently, help parents educate their children, and help ordinary people reclaim time from repetitive work. Silicon Valley spends huge amounts of energy talking about parameters, compute, benchmarks, valuations, and efficiency, but the more important question is much simpler: does this technology actually make people more capable and improve their lives?
